common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse ser (permanent characteristics, identity, profession) with estar (location, temporary states, emotions). Common errors include 'soy cansado' for 'I am tired' (should be 'estoy cansado') and 'estoy profesor' for 'I am a teacher' (should be 'soy profesor'). This distinction has no French equivalent.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (verbs, ser and estar), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students use por and para interchangeably without grasping the distinction (por = cause/reason/exchange/duration; para = purpose/destination/deadline/recipient). Edexcel writing tasks penalise this in mark schemes for accuracy. This distinction has no French equivalent.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (prepositions), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students default to the preterite for all past actions, missing the imperfect for repeated/ongoing past states (e.g. 'cuando era pequeño' not 'cuando fui pequeño'). Spanish requires this distinction; French collapses both into the perfect tense, so transferring habits from French AQA pedagogy fails here.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (preterite, imperfect), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students default adjectives to masculine singular even when the noun is feminine or plural (e.g. 'la casa es bonito' instead of 'bonita'). Gender of nouns is frequently misremembered, particularly with words ending in -a that are masculine (el problema, el día, el clima).
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (adjective agreement), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students translate word-for-word, producing English structures (e.g. 'tengo 15 años' is rendered as 'soy 15 años', missing the avoir-style tener idiom; 'me gusta el fútbol' is rendered without the definite article).
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Paper 4 Writing — sentences requiring translation into Spanish, qualifications.pearson.com/1SP1

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students transcribe Spanish phonemes using English spelling intuition — confusing b/v (which sound identical in Spanish), missing the silent h (hola = 'ola'), confusing c+e/i with z (both /θ/ in peninsular Spanish), and failing to write accents on stressed syllables that break default stress patterns.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Paper 2 Section B (Dictation, 10 marks), qualifications.pearson.com/1SP1

common_misconceptions.topic: Reflexive verbs in past and present
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students drop the reflexive pronoun or place it incorrectly (e.g. 'levanto' instead of 'me levanto'), and forget that the pronoun must move with the verb in negative commands and modal constructions ('voy a levantarme' or 'me voy a levantar').
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (reflexive verbs), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.topic: Definite article with abstract nouns and general statements
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students omit the definite article in contexts where Spanish requires it (e.g. 'La salud es importante' not 'Salud es importante'; 'Me gusta el deporte' not 'Me gusta deporte').
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (determiners), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students forget the personal a before a definite human direct object (e.g. 'veo a mi hermano' not 'veo mi hermano'). This has no French or English equivalent and is a high-frequency Spanish error.
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Specification — Appendix 2 Grammar (prepositions, personal a), qualifications.pearson.com

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students prepare scripted answers and freeze when prompts deviate. Edexcel role-plays are always set in one of nine prescribed transactional settings (café/restaurant, shop, hotel, train station, tourist info, cinema/theatre, campsite, leisure centre, doctor's surgery, in town).
common_misconceptions.source: Pearson Edexcel GCSE Spanish 1SP1 Paper 1 Speaking — role play (10 marks, transactional), qualifications.pearson.com/1SP1

student_errors_by_question_type.Dictation (Paper 2 Section B): Students lose marks by spelling Spanish words phonetically using English conventions. b/v confusion, missing accents on stressed syllables, and h/silent-h errors are frequent error hotspots. Source: Edexcel 1SP1 Paper 2 Section B is worth 10 marks at both Foundation and Higher tiers.
student_errors_by_question_type.Translation into English (Paper 3 Sectio: Students over-literal translate (e.g. 'tengo hambre' as 'I have hunger' instead of 'I am hungry') and miss the tener + noun idioms. They also lose marks for key-message omissions when they skip a clause they don't understand. Source: Edexcel 1SP1 Paper 3 Section B Translation, 10 marks.
student_errors_by_question_type.Translation into Spanish (Paper 4): Students produce English structures and forget gender agreement. They also confuse ser/estar, miss the personal a, and under-use the preterite/imperfect distinction (defaulting to one tense). Source: Edexcel 1SP1 Paper 4 Writing — translation task into Spanish.
student_errors_by_question_type.Role-play (Paper 1 Task 2): Students hesitate at the unpredictable question, give one-word answers rather than full sentences, and over-rely on memorised scripts. The role-play is set in a prescribed transactional setting (café, hotel, train station, tourist info, etc.) — students must respond flexibly to prompts. Source: Edexcel 1SP1 Paper 1 Task 2 Role Play, 10 marks (Foundation and Higher).
student_errors_by_question_type.Picture card and conversation (Paper 1 T: Students describe only what they see (present tense observations) and fail to extend to past (preterite/imperfect) and future tenses or opinions, which are needed to access higher marks. Source: Edexcel 1SP1 Paper 1 Task 3 — picture description (12 marks) plus broader conversation (16 marks).
student_errors_by_question_type.Open writing tasks (Paper 4): Students write in one tense throughout, under-use connectives and subordinate clauses, and avoid the subjunctive even where Higher-tier mark schemes reward it. Tier-specific word counts reward range over ambition. Source: Edexcel 1SP1 Paper 4 Writing structure.

topic_weighting_notes: All four papers are equally weighted at 25%. Drilling should be balanced across skills — not weighted toward content knowledge.

Theme 1 (My personal world) and Theme 2 (Lifestyle and wellbeing) provide the richest vocabulary for the Writing and Speaking papers because students can draw on personal experience. Drill them early and revisit across all units.

Theme 6 (Travel and tourism) is the highest-yield theme for preterite and imperfect practice since past-holiday narratives are a staple of writing prompts and picture cards. Spanish requires both tenses where French uses just the perfect.
Theme 4 (Media and technology) and Theme 3 (My neighbourhood) provide the strongest opportunity for opinion structures, comparatives and relative pronouns at Higher tier.

Sound-symbol correspondences are tested in both the Dictation section of Paper 2 and the Read Aloud task of Paper 1. They are a high-stakes area in the new specification, especially b/v, h/silent-h and accented syllables.

Higher tier vocabulary adds an additional layer on top of Foundation — focus Higher-only problems on the additional grammar (present subjunctive after key conjunctions, pluperfect tense, complex relative pronouns, future perfect) rather than just more words.

Equality (Theme 1) and mental wellbeing (Theme 2) are pitched at Higher tier in this plan because they require abstract opinion language and Higher-tier vocab including the present subjunctive after impersonal expressions.
current_spec_changes: First teaching September 2024, first exams 2026. The 1SP1 specification replaces the legacy Edexcel Spanish GCSE.
Dictation is now a distinct section of Paper 2 (10 marks at both tiers). Source: Edexcel 1SP1 Paper 2 Section B.
Read Aloud is a new task in Paper 1 Speaking. Foundation 35–40 words in 5 sentences; Higher 50–55 words in 4 sentences. Source: Edexcel 1SP1 Paper 1 Task 1.
Vocabulary is prescribed in Appendix 1 of the specification at Foundation and Higher tiers; texts will be built from this list.

Role plays are restricted to nine prescribed transactional settings (café/restaurant, shop, hotel, train station, tourist info, cinema/theatre, campsite, leisure centre, doctor's surgery, in town). Source: Edexcel 1SP1 Paper 1 Task 2.
Six broad thematic contexts replace earlier topic structures: My personal world, Lifestyle and wellbeing, My neighbourhood, Media and technology, Studying and my future, Travel and tourism.
Issue 2 (May 2025) clarified plural-noun rules, expanded reflexive-pronoun requirements at Foundation, and moved antes de + infinitive and después de + infinitive from Higher tier to Foundation tier.
pedagogical_notes: EEF evidence supports phonics-based instruction in MFL even at secondary level: systematically teaching sound-symbol correspondences in isolation then in cluster words improves transcription and reading-aloud accuracy. For Spanish this is especially powerful because spelling is highly phonemic once the SSCs are mastered. Source: educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/phonics.

Retrieval practice is particularly effective for vocabulary retention: short, frequent low-stakes recall beats massed practice. This justifies the Bronze/Silver/Gold practice format with spaced re-exposure. Source: EEF blog 'Why bother with retrieval?', educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk.

NCELP (National Centre for Excellence for Language Pedagogy) recommends a phonics-vocabulary-grammar framework where each item is introduced through its sound, then meaning, then grammatical behaviour. Practice lessons should reflect this by surfacing pronunciation before vocab drilling. Source: ncelp.org/phonics-collection.

Metacognitive strategies (planning what vocab to use, monitoring errors during writing, evaluating after) transfer well to MFL. Worked examples should include a brief 'what I'd check' step to model this. Source: EEF blog 'Metacognition in modern foreign language teaching', educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk.

AI-marked translation and role-play questions should reward communicative success (key message through) over perfect accuracy — exam mark schemes do this. Minor gender, ser/estar slips or missing accents should not prevent reward if the key idea is communicated.

Spanish-specific pedagogical priority: contrast Spanish with English AND with French where students are doing both. The ser/estar and por/para distinctions, the preterite/imperfect contrast, and the personal a have no French or English parallel and need explicit drilling — students cannot transfer intuition from another language.

lessons_in_batch.title: TV, Film and Streaming
lessons_in_batch.description: TV programmes, film genres and streaming preferences using opinion phrases and the preterite.
spec_references: Theme: Media and technology (TV and film)
Appendix 2: Grammar — preterite tense regular verbs, opinion phrases

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: AQA bundles music/film/TV in one lesson. Split here — focus this lesson on TV and film only, with streaming as the modern angle Edexcel emphasises. Note: Spanish typically uses preterite (vi una película) for past viewing rather than perfect.

lessons_in_batch.title: Music and Listening Habits
lessons_in_batch.description: Music genres, listening habits and concerts using comparative structures.
spec_references: Appendix 2: Grammar — comparatives más/menos que, present tense, desde hace + present

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Pull music vocab from AQA L2 'Music, Film and TV'; build fresh drills focused only on music habits and instruments. Drill 'desde hace + present' (escucho música desde hace cinco años) — Spanish uses present, not perfect, for ongoing duration.

lessons_in_batch.title: Social Media and Online Life
lessons_in_batch.description: Social media platforms, daily use and the advantages and disadvantages of being online.
spec_references: Appendix 2: Grammar — relative pronouns que/quien, modal verbs poder/deber

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Direct lift from Spanish AQA Pop Culture L8 'Social Media and Online Life'. Note: Spanish AQA places social-media content in Popular Culture (not Communication and World — French AQA's location). Reuse balanced-opinion structures and relative-pronoun drills.

lessons_in_batch.title: Gaming and Digital Entertainment
lessons_in_batch.description: Video games, online gaming and digital habits using time markers and desde hace.
spec_references: Appendix 2: Grammar — desde hace + present, time markers

content_transfer.adaptation_notes: Spanish AQA bundles gaming under Pop Culture L1 'Free-Time Activities and Hobbies' (broader than French AQA's gaming-as-pop-culture-L3 framing). Pull only gaming-relevant vocab; build fresh drills with stronger digital-life focus.
